code.why: X's 404 for a path of pbs.twimg.com, video.twimg.com or abs.twimg.com that is none of the three shapes this screen serves. The descriptor routes to the screen only the paths its hosts' patterns name (X_PBS_PATHS, X_VIDEO_PATHS, X_ABS_PATHS), and each matches one of the screen's three readers, so no World's router hands it such a path.

The crawl of a post's link when the runtime cannot make the request at all (ctx.ask throws: a host with no route out for it). The walk answers the crawl with the life's application answers (the Model Editor's page), and a World that cannot reach a page answers it unreachable without throwing, so no World the life runs in reaches this; it keeps a host that throws from failing the post, which then shows no card, as X's does for a page it could not read.

A sign-in asked to return the person to an address on another site (an open redirect, which X's sign-in does not follow): the person is sent home instead. Every return address in this life is X's own (a page of x.com, an authorize screen on api.x.com), which the screens that send a person to sign in write themselves.
The host listener is started by the CLI/runtime; a World fetch walk has no listening process to start or stop.
An unexpected failure of rendering/storage in the host. Documented authorization request errors and cancellations use errorPage/redirectError and remain in the walk.
Used only by answerOfFailure for unexpected resource-request host exceptions.
World-only setup: issuing a preconfigured token without the customer consent flow. This is not an X API request or documented vendor refusal.
Default callbacks selected by the World app-registration door when setup gives no callback; Dub registers its explicit callback.
An approved request token names an account the account door already made, and no served X API deletes that account. Only inconsistent host state could lose it between consent and exchange.

A peer posting an absent or settled internal consent handle. The current page generates a fresh handle, posts once, and redirects away; this is the substitute form protocol, not an X-documented API refusal. The unreachable duplicate refusal on the machine is removed; the public single-use OAuth code refusal remains served and replayed.

The World application's credentials (the descriptor's credentialDoor), which the runtime asks for at boot and fills into the application's TWITTER_ names: the developer console's App, its owner's personal Access Token and its OAuth 2.0 client, which no X API makes. The life's own Apps are registered at the console doors it walks (oauth1Apps, clients); the customer entry (journeys/first-use.json) is what signs with these.

The seeding doors' refusals of what a World was asked to seed (a body that is no JSON object, a handle that is no X handle, an id another account or post holds, a profile picture that is no https URL, a password without its email, an email another account's person holds, a post or engagement naming an account or post the World does not hold) and the retirement of an account's earlier person when it is seeded again with another email: World setup, not X's API, and this life seeds each account once, well formed.

An exception thrown out of a handler: the host's own failure (a 500), or the decode a malformed HTTP Basic credential raises at the token endpoint. Dub builds its Basic from its two keys (callback/route.ts:110) and the root's exchange from its custody, so no request of a World raises one; the host process answers it so a fault never escapes the fetch.
X's authorize page for a request token it does not hold or has settled: each authorize or authenticate screen this story opens is the one its App's request token was just issued for.
